words: All the living things in a place and the non-living things they depend on, like water, soil, and sunlight.
Harmful materials that get into the air, water, or soil and make it hard for living things to survive.
A plant or animal from somewhere else that spreads in a new place and harms the living things that belong there.
When the natural home of plants and animals is destroyed or changed so much that they can't live there anymore.
Rainwater that flows over the land, picking up things like fertilizer and carrying them into rivers, lakes, and wetlands.
The work of protecting and restoring nature so ecosystems stay healthy now and in the future.

parts.title: Florida's Wild Places Are Changing
parts.html: Florida's ecosystems, like the Everglades, mangrove coasts, and dry scrub, are home to hundreds of kinds of plants and animals. But scientists are watching these places change. Some lakes are turning green. Some animals are losing their homes. Scientists study these places closely to find out what is causing the changes.

parts.title: Three Big Threats
parts.html:
Pollution: rain washes fertilizer off farms and lawns. This runoff makes algae grow out of control, blocking sunlight and using up oxygen fish need.

Invasive species: Burmese pythons came as pets, and some got loose. Now they spread and eat native animals.

Habitat loss: when a wetland is drained or a forest is cleared, the animals there have nowhere to go.

parts.title: How Scientists Know, and How People Help
parts.html:
Scientists use evidence: observations and data. In places where pythons spread, they counted far fewer raccoons, opossums, and rabbits. Satellites show where algae covers a lake.

People are working on fixes. Engineers build filter marshes to clean water. Divers and trappers remove invaders. Parks and preserves protect wild land.

wow.title: Fixing the River of Grass
wow.alt: A wide, shallow marsh of grass and water stretching to the horizon
wow.caption: The Everglades' River of Grass · Everglades National Park
wow.html:
Long ago, people dug canals to drain water from the Everglades for farms and cities. Today, engineers are working to send clean water back.

It is one of the biggest repair jobs on Earth, and it will take many years. Nature doesn't heal overnight.
wow.insetCap: A steam dredge digging an Everglades canal, long ago.

keyIdea: Florida's ecosystems face three big threats: pollution, invasive species, and habitat loss. Runoff carries fertilizer into lakes and makes algae grow. Invasive species like pythons and lionfish spread and eat native animals. Habitat loss happens when wild land is cleared. Scientists use observations and data as evidence, and people are working on fixes: cleaning water, removing invaders, and protecting land.
